stories.notes: Empty acceptance criteria and null spec on a complex multi-market CMS live-preview feature. openspec must elaborate requirements and define AC first; speckit then hardens with testability, security, and edge-case coverage (latency, concurrent edits, fallback rendering).

agentContributions.notes: Live Preview is a novel capability. The primary attachment point is useContent (src/hooks/useContent.ts), which all content-consuming components call. The previous rejection flagged src/context/ContentstackContext.tsx and ContentstackProvider as non-existent in this codebase, so they are excluded from verificationCriteria and locationHint. Only files confirmed present in the CodeGraph source are referenced.

Openspec delivered an empty acceptanceCriteria array, so I authored the full set from scratch based on the story title ('Live Preview of Content in CMS'), the confirmed file paths across three codebases, and standard Contentstack Live Preview patterns. Key areas covered: (1) Detection of preview vs production context (AC-1, AC-2, AC-13), (2) Real-time content update with latency bound (AC-3, AC-8, AC-11, AC-12, AC-14), (3) Error handling for disconnect/reconnect (AC-4, AC-5), (4) Graceful fallback for deleted/unpublished entries (AC-9), (5) Security — no preview data leakage to production cache (AC-6), (6) Accessibility — live region announcements (AC-7), (7) Cross-codebase parity (AC-10). IMPORTANT CAVEAT: I have not seen the actual file contents. The criteria assume typical Contentstack Live Preview SDK integration patterns (iframe detection, WebSocket/polling channel, draft content delivery). If the actual implementation uses a different mechanism, some criteria may need adjustment. The context file name varies across codebases (.tsx vs .ts vs lowercase), which AC-10 accounts for by asserting behavioural parity rather than file-level identity.

coordinatorReview.reviewNotes: Openspec failed its primary mandate: coordinator notes explicitly instructed it to 'elaborate requirements and define AC first,' yet it delivered an empty acceptanceCriteria array. Its only value was reconnaissance (identifying useContent as the attachment point, excluding non-existent files from prior rejection). Speckit then overcompensated by authoring 14 acceptance criteria from scratch — doing openspec's job rather than its own (reviewing and hardening). While speckit's ACs are reasonably comprehensive (detection, real-time updates, error handling, fallback, security, accessibility, cross-codebase parity), it explicitly caveats that it has not seen actual file contents and assumes typical Contentstack Live Preview SDK patterns. The ACs may not match the real implementation mechanism. Both agents added value, but it was entirely one-sided and non-collaborative — openspec produced nothing actionable and speckit operated outside its intended role with unverified assumptions. A human must validate the ACs against actual codebase contents before implementation proceeds.
